subtype: Approach: picks an easier task when tired or upset [Thinking]
passage: I am Ayesha, and I had my science test tomorrow. My tummy felt fizzy and my head felt full. When I opened my book, the words swam. I thought, if I start now I will only cry. So I took my colour pencils and drew my favourite thing, a big elephant with a red hat. I drew for ten minutes and did not think about the test at all. My shoulders came down. Then I closed the drawing book and read the first chapter. It was easier, because my mind was quiet. Deepak, my brother, saw the elephant and said it looked funny. I said, "I know. It helped."

qa.a: Ayesha drew a big elephant with a red hat.

qa.q: How was Ayesha feeling before the test?
qa.a: Ayesha was worried, with a fizzy tummy and a full head.

qa.q: What else could Ayesha do if drawing does not help Ayesha calm down?
qa.a: Ayesha could ask Deepak or a parent to sit close for a few minutes, or take a short walk before starting.

qa.q: How might Deepak have seen Ayesha's drawing time?
qa.a: Deepak thought the elephant looked funny, and may have understood that it was a way of calming down.

grounding: Shows a child doing a favourite drawing for ten minutes to calm down before starting to revise.

subtype: Approach: picks an easier task when tired or upset [Thinking]
passage:
Note to Lavanya's class teacher, from her mother, Sangeeta

Just so you know about last night. Lavanya was very worried about today's science test. At seven she sat at the table, opened the book and closed it again. Then she said, "My head is too full. If I draw my cat for ten minutes, I'll be calmer, then I'll read." I let her. She set the kitchen timer herself, drew her cat curled on the chair, and when it rang she put the drawing away and revised for an hour. She was much calmer. I'm telling you because she worked out this trick on her own and I'd like her to keep it.

qa.a: Her cat curled on the chair.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling before she started drawing?
qa.a: She was very worried about the science test; she said her head was too full.

qa.q: How could the teacher support Lavanya's trick at school?
qa.a: The teacher could let her take a short calming moment before tests, and praise her for knowing what helps her.

qa.q: What would change if Sangeeta had insisted she start revising straight away?
qa.a: Lavanya might have stayed anxious and read without taking much in, instead of revising calmly for an hour.

grounding: A girl worried before a test does a favourite drawing for ten minutes to calm down, then begins revision.

subtype: Approach: picks an easier task when tired or upset [Thinking]
passage:
Wednesday

Maths test tomorrow and my tummy has been funny all evening. I opened my book and the numbers just swam. Varun said, "Just study, na, didi." Easy for him, he's in class two. But I thought: when I'm this worried, nothing goes in. When I draw, my hands stop shaking. So I made a deal with myself. Ten minutes of drawing, then maths. I drew the mango tree from our window, with a parrot in it. When the clock said ten minutes, I stopped, even though the parrot had no tail yet. Then I did fractions for forty minutes. I think I got most of them. The parrot can get its tail tomorrow after the test. Rajni, you're clever sometimes!

qa.a: The mango tree from the window, with a parrot in it.

qa.q: How did Rajni feel before she started drawing?
qa.a: Rajni felt very worried; her tummy had been funny and the numbers just swam.

qa.q: What else could Rajni try if drawing ever stops working?
qa.a: She could try a short walk or a few slow breaths, then start with the easiest sums first.

qa.q: Why might Varun see the problem differently?
qa.a: Varun is younger and has no big test, so he doesn't feel the worry and thinks she should just study.

grounding: A girl worried before a test draws for ten minutes to calm down, then begins revision.
